questions.question: According to the definitions in ISPE Baseline Guide Vol. 5, 2nd edition, what is the difference between Commissioning and Qualification?

options.A: Qualification is only document review, while Commissioning requires actual test execution, and the two are carried out by different teams
options.B: Qualification adds Quality Unit oversight on top of commissioning, with a focus on risk to product quality
options.C: Commissioning applies only to equipment and Qualification only to facilities and utilities, so their scopes do not overlap
options.D: Commissioning is executed by the supplier, while Qualification is reviewed by the regulatory authority, which issues a certificate

questions.explanation: The guide states explicitly that the only difference is that Qualification has Quality Unit oversight and focuses on the system's risk to product quality; the Quality Unit makes the final decision on whether the system is fit for intended use. Both require actual testing, and both cover all types of systems.

questions.question: Which of the following best matches this guide's definition of a CDE (Critical Design Element)?

options.A: A process parameter whose variability impacts a CQA and therefore must be monitored or controlled, with its range established during process validation
options.B: A physical, chemical, or microbiological property that must be within an appropriate limit, range, or distribution to ensure drug product quality, and that is tested at release
options.C: The final report document, approved by the Quality Unit, that formally releases the system and compiles all test results
options.D: A design function or feature of a system that is necessary to consistently manufacture a product of the intended quality, and that is verified through C&Q

questions.explanation: A CDE is a design function or feature of an engineered system, such as automated alarms and data management, or components, instruments, and materials, and it is verified during C&Q. The definition of "a process parameter that impacts a CQA and must be monitored" is the CPP, and "a physical, chemical, or microbiological property tested at release" is the CQA; both are easily confused with the CDE.

questions.question: What is the main reason the 2nd edition no longer requires a Component Criticality Assessment for every system component?

options.A: Because CDEs are an output of the System Risk Assessment, so there is no need to assess component criticality one by one
options.B: Because all components are considered non-critical in the 2nd edition, so there is no need to verify their functions separately
options.C: Because this work has been fully replaced by supplier FAT, so the owner need not perform any verification or keep any related records
options.D: Because the V-Model has integrated component assessment into the IQ protocol, with IQ covering all components one by one

questions.explanation: The guide explains that CDEs are an output of the System Risk Assessment, so component criticality no longer needs to be assessed. The same passage also notes that the V-Model has been replaced by different flow diagrams and that the term "Indirect Impact" is no longer used; only direct impact and not direct impact are distinguished.

questions.question: A test result deviates from specification, affects a CDE, and cannot be corrected directly. According to this guide's terminology, how should it be handled?

options.A: Treat it as an ordinary discrepancy, which can be closed once the executor annotates it and the supervisor signs
options.B: Close it with joint approval by the engineering SME and the system owner, without Quality Unit involvement
options.C: It is a deviation and must be approved by the Quality Unit before it can be closed
options.D: It need not be recorded as an exception separately; as long as the retest passes, the new result replaces the original one

questions.explanation: In this guide, a deviation is a departure from specification, or a critical discrepancy that affects a CA/CDE and cannot be corrected, and it requires Quality Unit approval before closure. A discrepancy is the broader notion of being outside the expected range or not meeting a requirement and does not necessarily require Quality Unit approval.

questions.question: According to 1.6.3, what role does the guide expect the Quality Unit to play in the C&Q process?

options.A: The Quality Unit decides the technical details of how systems are designed and tested, and leads the execution of all tests
options.B: As a member of the C&Q team, it approves the plans, documents, and final qualified status of systems that impact product quality
options.C: It becomes involved only after system release, keeping the documents and performing periodic record archiving
options.D: It reviews all engineering documents word for word to make sure there are no typographical or formatting errors, and is responsible for all sign-offs

questions.explanation: The Quality Unit takes part in the process, approves the plans and documents for systems that impact product quality, and approves the final qualified status. The guide states clearly that this is a Quality Assurance role, not documentation quality control; how systems are designed and tested is the responsibility of SMEs, because the Quality Unit need not be expert in every manufacturing system.

questions.topic: What a URS should not contain
questions.question: Which of the following should NOT be written as a URS requirement statement?

options.A: A verifiable statement of the range and accuracy of a controlled parameter, for example a temperature setpoint range
options.B: Alarm requirements, identifying which alarms are critical to product quality
options.C: Data integrity and data storage/display requirements, classified by requirement source and category
options.D: A general statement such as "must comply with all GxP regulations"

questions.explanation: A URS should not contain general statements (such as complying with local regulations or all GxP), design details, operating sequences, or unverifiable parameters. Verifiable ranges of controlled parameters, alarm requirements, and data integrity requirements are all content the guide lists as belonging in a URS.

questions.question: According to 2.3, who should approve the URS, and under what circumstances may the Quality Unit be excused from approving it?

options.A: The system owner, SMEs, and the Quality Unit; if the Quality Unit has already approved the source documents of the quality requirements, it need not approve the URS
options.B: Only the Quality Unit; this can never be omitted, whether or not the source documents of the quality requirements have been approved
options.C: The system owner and the supplier; the Quality Unit signs only at system release and does not take part at the URS stage
options.D: The project manager and SMEs; if the system is direct impact, the supplier approves on their behalf, and the Quality Unit only needs to be informed afterwards

questions.explanation: The URS is approved by the system owner, appropriate SMEs, and the Quality Unit; however, if the source documents of the quality requirements (for example, the source of the CQAs and CPPs) have already been approved by the Quality Unit, the Quality Unit does not need to approve the URS again. Changes after URS approval must go through change management.

questions.question: Of the eight decision questions in Table 3.1, how many must be answered YES for the system to be classified as a direct impact system?

options.A: All eight
options.B: At least three
options.C: At least one
options.D: A majority, that is, at least five

questions.explanation: A YES answer to any one question means the system is a direct impact system. A direct impact system requires commissioning and qualification, while a not direct impact system requires only commissioning. The questions support the decision and do not replace the professional judgment of qualified personnel.

questions.question: A system produces WFI for use in the process, and WFI that does not meet specification could affect finished product quality. Which decision question in Table 3.1 does this correspond to most directly?

options.A: Q5: the system establishes the environment required for the process, such as nitrogen blanketing, temperature, and humidity control
options.B: Q3: the system provides excipients, or produces ingredients or solvents (such as WFI) that affect the finished product
options.C: Q6: the system uses or stores electronic record data regulated by 21 CFR Part 11
options.D: Q8: the system provides product identification information, such as labeling content like lot number and expiry date

questions.explanation: Q3 specifically addresses systems that provide excipients or produce ingredients and solvents (WFI is the example), and considers whether they might introduce microorganisms, corrosion products, and the like. A YES answer classifies the system as a direct impact system.

questions.question: Which of the following is consistent with this guide regarding the definition of system boundaries?

options.A: Defined early in the project (at the BOD stage), recorded and marked on the P&ID or PFD, and together covering the entire project
options.B: Defined when IQ is executed, and always based on the supplier's scope of supply, with no marking on drawings needed
options.C: Decided by the Quality Unit alone at the PQ stage and recorded in the test report
options.D: Defined at the release stage, to decide which reports will be issued, who signs each report, and how they are filed

questions.explanation: System boundaries should be defined early, at the BOD stage, so that the list of systems can be established and the System Risk Assessment performed, and the systems must together cover the entire project scope. The supplier's scope of supply is often used as the basis but should be examined carefully, because dividing the boundaries differently may be more advantageous.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of the System Risk Assessment?

options.A: To replace the URS as the sole requirements document for the system, serving directly as the basis for all tests, acceptance criteria, and release decisions
options.B: To assess and rank the criticality of every component in the system, and then decide the depth of testing required for each component
options.C: To apply QRM to direct impact systems, identify CAs/CDEs and procedural controls, and reduce risk
options.D: To assess whether suppliers are qualified to provide documentation, and decide the frequency and scope of supplier audits

questions.explanation: The System Risk Assessment is a QRM review of the controls on product quality risk in a direct impact system, identifying CAs/CDEs and procedural controls. Ranking components one by one is a practice retired in the 2nd edition; CDEs are identified directly from the System Risk Assessment.

questions.question: Which of the following is the process for performing a System Risk Assessment?

options.A: One large cross-functional team completes it from start to finish in a single pass, with no phases and no draft documents first
options.B: The supplier completes the risk assessment independently, and after Quality Unit approval it is adopted directly, with no review or additions by the owner
options.C: The team first assigns risk levels, then goes back to find corresponding controls, and writes the process description last
options.D: A small team first prepares a baseline draft, and a broader team then reviews it and assigns the risk profile

questions.explanation: The guide recommends two stages: a small team builds a baseline draft, and a broader team reviews the content for gaps and assigns the risk profile. With adequate preparation, each of the two meetings should take no more than a few hours. Risk levels are assigned only after the sources of risk and the controls have been identified.

questions.question: After review, an SME finds that a control for a high risk is unsuitable (for example, its implementation cost exceeds the loss if the risk occurs) and recommends accepting the system's high risk. How should this be handled according to the guide?

options.A: SME sign-off is enough, and no other approval is needed
options.B: The assessment must be accepted by senior management
options.C: Agreement from a single person in the Quality Unit is sufficient
options.D: The high risk is automatically downgraded to medium because of the SME's recommendation

questions.explanation: High risk is generally not acceptable and must be reduced through design or procedural controls. However, if the SME judges the control inappropriate and recommends acceptance, the assessment must be accepted by senior management. Medium risk may be accepted when the SME considers it acceptable for the specific process.

questions.question: Is a periodic review of the System Risk Assessment required during the operational phase?

options.A: No time-based periodic review; it is reassessed only on deviations related to system performance, and reviewed together with the URS when changes are made
options.B: A full reassessment is required once a year, with the review report signed by the Quality Unit and filed, whether or not the system has changed
options.C: It is reviewed only once before system retirement, and the review result is included in the retirement report for future reference
options.D: It must be redone after every preventive maintenance, updating all related risk levels and controls

questions.explanation: The guide states explicitly that the System Risk Assessment is not subject to time-based periodic review; a more efficient approach is to reassess when a deviation related to system performance occurs. Any system change requires review of both the URS and the System Risk Assessment under change management.

questions.question: After the System Risk Assessment is complete, how should the identified design controls (CAs/CDEs) and procedural controls each be handled?

options.A: Both stay only within the System Risk Assessment and are not put into any other document, to avoid duplicating documents and simplify management
options.B: Procedural controls are written into the URS, while design controls are listed only in SOPs, with the user department responsible for later maintenance and updates
options.C: Design controls are kept by the supplier in its document system, while procedural controls are held separately by the Quality Unit
options.D: Design controls are updated into the URS (or just added to the Traceability Matrix), and procedural controls are brought into the C&Q Plan

questions.explanation: Design controls (CAs/CDEs) are treated as system requirements and must be updated into the URS, or just added to the Matrix when a Traceability Matrix is used. Procedural controls must be brought into the scope of the C&Q Plan. The guide also reminds that most risk controls are achieved through design, and procedural controls are not as robust as design controls.

questions.question: According to Chapter 5, what is the relationship between Design Review (DR) and Design Qualification (DQ)?

options.A: DQ and DR are not separate, independent activities; DQ focuses on CAs/CDEs and is approved by the Quality Unit
options.B: DQ is completely independent of DR and may start only one year after all DR is finished, and is executed by a different team
options.C: DR and DQ both apply to all systems, use the same document format, and both require item-by-item repeated review
options.D: DR covers only critical design, whereas DQ covers critical and non-critical design; their scopes do not overlap at all, and they must be executed separately

questions.explanation: DR and DQ are not two independent things; DQ is a standalone document focused on CAs/CDEs and approved by the Quality Unit. DR covers both critical and non-critical design aspects, while DQ applies only to direct impact systems, so "DR covers only critical design, whereas DQ covers critical and non-critical design" has it exactly backwards.

questions.question: Which of the following is consistent with the guide regarding Quality Unit participation in design reviews?

options.A: Quality Unit attendance is mandatory for both kinds of design review, and the review is invalid if it is absent
options.B: Quality Unit attendance is not needed for either kind of design review, and engineering SMEs take full responsibility for the review
options.C: For the review focused on engineering design, attendance is optional; for the review focused on quality, attendance is strongly recommended and documented
options.D: For the review focused on engineering design, attendance is strongly recommended and documented; for the review focused on quality, it is optional

questions.explanation: The engineering design review focuses on operability, maintainability, and safety, and Quality Unit attendance is optional there, although it helps streamline DQ. The quality-focused review concentrates on regulatory compliance and CAs/CDEs that affect product quality, and Quality Unit attendance is strongly recommended, with the review documented.

questions.question: Which statement about a formal protocol for DQ is correct?

options.A: Regulations explicitly require a pre-approved formal DQ protocol, and without one the DQ has no validity
options.B: A formal protocol is not a regulatory requirement, but the DQ execution plan, scope, and Quality Unit approval must be defined
options.C: DQ may only be done once after all design is complete, and may not be phased or done system by system, nor refer to design review results
options.D: DQ can be approved by the SME alone, without the Quality Unit, as long as the sign-off record is kept

questions.explanation: The guide explains that using a formal protocol to compare requirements against design item by item is not a regulatory requirement, but the DQ plan, scope, and Quality Unit approval must still be defined. A small project may do the DQ once after all design is complete, while a large project may do it by area or function as each part of the design is completed.

questions.question: Who should approve the final DQ report declaring the design fit for intended use?

options.A: The supplier and the project manager, with the project manager signing the report on behalf of both the owner and the supplier
options.B: Only the Quality Unit, with other departments merely reviewing and not signing the report
options.C: Engineering and Operations, excluding the Quality Unit, to speed up report approval
options.D: Appropriate representatives of Engineering, Manufacturing, and the Quality Unit

questions.explanation: The final DQ report states that the design is fit for intended use and is approved by representatives at an appropriate level from Engineering, Manufacturing, and the Quality Unit. DQ is a document in which the Quality Unit takes part in approval, which is also what distinguishes it from ordinary design review documents.

questions.question: Before DQ is performed, which of the following is a prerequisite that should already be in place?

options.A: The system's IQ and OQ are complete, and the related reports have been approved by the Quality Unit
options.B: The system has arrived on site and SAT is complete, and all on-site installation verifications have been signed off
options.C: Design review is complete, and all design issues affecting CAs/CDEs, CPPs, and CQAs have been closed
options.D: PQ batches are complete and approved, and batch records and trend analyses have been reviewed

questions.explanation: The prerequisites for DQ include the URS, the System Risk Assessment, and a completed design review, with confirmation that all open design issues affecting CAs/CDEs, CPPs, and CQAs have been closed. IQ, SAT, and PQ are all activities that occur after design confirmation.

questions.question: What should the approval sequence of the C&Q Plan and the test documents be?

options.A: Approve the test documents first, and approve the C&Q Plan after execution is complete, to shorten the schedule
options.B: The C&Q Plan is approved before the test documents, and the test documents must be approved before execution
options.C: The C&Q Plan is approved at the same time as the final report, and the test documents are signed after execution
options.D: The C&Q Plan is approved only after PQ is complete, as a retrospective document for the whole project

questions.explanation: The C&Q Plan must be approved before the corresponding test instructions, and the test instructions must in turn be approved before the tests that support validation begin execution. The plan should also state how existing test documents and results from commissioning (including FAT and SAT) will be referenced in validation.

questions.topic: Is a separate C&Q Plan always required
questions.question: A company is adding a small system. According to the explanation in 6.2, which of the following approaches is most consistent with the guide?

options.A: A separate C&Q Plan is not always needed; the requirements can be incorporated into the change control plan
options.B: A separate C&Q Plan must always be written and approved page by page by the Quality Unit
options.C: The decision on whether a C&Q Plan is needed can be made only after PQ is complete
options.D: It can only be incorporated into the Validation Master Plan, and not into any other document

questions.explanation: The guide states that a separate C&Q Plan is not always required; C&Q planning can be incorporated into a validation plan or into change control, for example into change control when a small system is added. More complex projects (such as a filling line with terminal sterilization and secondary packaging) are better suited to a separate plan.

questions.question: Regarding whether supplier FAT/SAT results can be used for validation, how should the C&Q Plan address this at the planning stage?

options.A: Never accept supplier test results; all items are re-executed on site by the owner and signed off
options.B: Wait until all testing is complete, then decide from the actual results which supplier test results to accept, without explaining this in advance in the plan
options.C: Engineering decides during execution whether to use supplier results, with no basis recorded in advance
options.D: Decide at planning which FAT, SAT, or commissioning results can be used to demonstrate qualification, and reduce duplicate testing according to criticality

questions.explanation: The guide asks for early identification of documentation sources and, at planning, a decision on which existing test results can be used to demonstrate that the system is qualified, based on the supplier assessment and the criticality of the tests, with the aim of minimizing retesting. Documents need not be perfect, but they must be easy to understand.

questions.question: For sterilization and cleaning cycle development, what does the guide recommend about the timing of final validation testing?

options.A: Complete final validation testing first and then perform cycle development, so parameters can be adjusted and confirmed at the same time
options.B: Do both at the same time with no need to distinguish their order, and handle all changes together in the PQ report with an explanation
options.C: Perform final validation testing after cycle development is complete, with changes in between handled through ECM
options.D: Cycle development is entirely outside the scope of C&Q and should be handled by the production unit on its own

questions.explanation: Cycle development may reveal factors that need validation or change what is validated, so final validation testing is recommended after cycle development, allowing changes to be handled through Engineering Change Management. Whether cycle development is included in C&Q is decided and documented by each organization.

questions.question: The C&Q Plan needs adjustment while the project is under way. Which of the following approaches is consistent with the guide?

options.A: Major adjustments must be approved by the original approvers or their delegates, with revision history kept; minor deviations are recorded with justification in the summary report
options.B: Any minor deviation must first be handled by revising the C&Q Plan, or execution may not continue, and the Quality Unit must reapprove it
options.C: The C&Q Plan must be revised with every update to the integrated schedule and sent again to all original approvers for sign-off
options.D: Once approved, the C&Q Plan may never be changed; a new plan must be written and all tests must be redone

questions.explanation: The C&Q Plan must be updated as project information evolves; revisions are approved by the original approvers or their delegates, revision history is maintained, and change management is used. Minor deviations do not necessarily require revision and can be recorded with appropriate justification in the Qualification Summary Report. Updates to the integrated schedule also should not prompt revision of the plan.

questions.question: What is the difference between Pre-Delivery Inspection (PDI) and Receipt Inspection (RI)?

options.A: PDI is performed at the owner's site and RI at the supplier's factory, and both are performed by the owner's QA
options.B: PDI is used only for software systems and RI only for mechanical equipment, and their record formats and approval processes also differ
options.C: They are the same thing under different company names, with identical timing and inspection content, so there is no need to distinguish them
options.D: PDI inspects the system or components at the supplier before shipment; RI confirms at the owner's site after delivery that what arrived meets requirements

questions.explanation: PDI is construction inspection and testing performed at the supplier before delivery; it can catch problems early and also allows inspection of parts that cannot be seen after assembly (for example, baffles inside a heating jacket). RI confirms immediately on arrival that the delivered items meet requirements, and nonconforming items are quarantined for disposition.

questions.question: Which of the following is consistent with the guide regarding the content and format of the Turnover Package (TOP)?

options.A: The supplier decides the format and content entirely, and the owner need not agree on any requirements before placing the order
options.B: The content should be agreed by the parties before the order is placed, and the owner should define a standard format consistent with its document control
options.C: Only direct impact systems need a TOP
options.D: Once approved, the TOP may not be updated, and any addition or change must be handled as a new project

questions.explanation: The content of the TOP should be agreed by the parties before the order is placed, so that document delivery does not later become a project risk, and the owner should define a standard format that fits its document control. The guide also says a TOP should be obtained for all systems in operation, with later updates handled under change management.

questions.question: Which of the following is consistent with the guide regarding the prerequisites for PQ testing?

options.A: Cycle development is done after installation and operational testing are complete, and only then is PQ testing performed
options.B: PQ should be performed before operational testing, to find process problems early and shorten the overall schedule
options.C: Cycle development should be completed at the same time as installation testing, after which PQ can be skipped as appropriate
options.D: PQ can fully replace operational testing, so only one of the two needs to be performed, as decided by the SME

questions.explanation: The guide requires installation and operational testing (as applicable) to be completed first, confirming that the system operates properly, before cycle development, after which PQ testing can be performed. PQ verifies that the system operates effectively and reproducibly according to the process method and product specifications.

questions.question: What range should operational/functional testing cover?

options.A: Only the nominal setpoint; the rest of the operating range and alarm behavior is guaranteed by the supplier and need not be verified separately on site
options.B: Only the normal operating mode, excluding alarm and failure mode testing, to shorten overall test time
options.C: The expected normal operating range (including upper and lower limits), normal and alarm/failure modes, and worst-case conditions where necessary
options.D: Only the specification values listed in the supplier's catalog, without separately defining operating ranges or alarm conditions

questions.explanation: Operational testing must show that the system performs its specified functions across the expected operating range, including the upper and lower operating limits, normal and alarm/failure modes, and worst-case conditions. If the systems are interconnected (for example, a packaging line), integrated operation of the whole line must also be confirmed.

questions.question: While testing a WFI system, the loop return pressure fails to meet the acceptance criterion and no cause can be found. Return pressure is a CA, and negative pressure represents a risk of contaminating the loop. How should this be handled?

options.A: The SME accepts it directly after noting the rationale on the record, and explains it together in the summary report, with no discrepancy form raised
options.B: The design authority accepts the result and signs the test record, and it can be closed with no other procedure
options.C: Change the expected result and acceptance criterion so that the test result meets the criterion, and update the test document version
options.D: Treat it as a critical discrepancy, document the investigation on a discrepancy form, and close it only after Quality Unit approval

questions.explanation: A discrepancy related to CAs/CDEs is a critical issue and needs Quality Unit approval before closure; when an acceptance criterion is not met and the cause is unknown, the investigation results and adjustments should be recorded on a discrepancy form. What an SME or design authority may accept is a missed engineering expected result, not a quality requirement.

questions.question: What does the Acceptance and Release stage represent?

options.A: The final closing of all project documents, after which the system needs no further review, change control, or maintenance
options.B: The end of the supplier's contractual responsibility, after which no technical support, spare parts, or warranty service is provided
options.C: The start of the "qualified state," and the starting point for QA-managed change control, ongoing monitoring, and periodic review
options.D: The start of PQ, after which the system's validation activities and process simulation batches can formally begin and trending is started

questions.explanation: Release marks the start of the qualified state and the beginning of QA-managed Quality Change Control, continuous performance monitoring, and periodic review. The guide also explains that this stage is not a catch-all mechanism for closing out all system or project documents.

questions.question: What is the principle for handling discrepancies at release?

options.A: Those affecting product quality must be closed before release; the rest may stay open under an approved action plan
options.B: No discrepancy may remain open under any circumstances; even those unrelated to product quality must be closed first
options.C: As long as the engineering SME agrees, discrepancies affecting product quality may also remain open
options.D: All discrepancies may remain open, to be tracked and handled by the operating unit after release

questions.explanation: Discrepancies affecting product quality must be documented, addressed, retested if necessary, and closed successfully before release can be completed. Those not affecting product quality may remain open, but there must be an approved action plan, an owner, and a deadline, and their status is listed in the summary report. Releasing with open items is a Quality Unit decision.

questions.question: For a system with CAs/CDEs, which of the following is an example of a quality system element that must be in place before release?

options.A: A complete process validation (PPQ) batch report that has passed Quality Unit review
options.B: Video footage of the supplier's FAT, stored in the owner's document control system
options.C: A revised version of the customer contract, with attached price and terms related to commercial supply
options.D: Calibration and maintenance systems and procedures, and a mechanism (such as a logbook) to track usage and maintenance

questions.explanation: A system with CAs/CDEs must have quality system elements implemented before it is released for production, such as calibration/maintenance systems and procedures, a mechanism to track usage and maintenance (a logbook), and supplier documentation, so that the system can remain in a qualified state. The summary report must state that these elements are in place.

questions.topic: Acceptance and release report for large projects
questions.question: In a large project with multiple interconnected systems, each system has been tested and closed out separately. What is the function of the overall acceptance and release report at this point?

options.A: To list again every system's test descriptions, results, and acceptance criteria, and re-execute sampling confirmation item by item
options.B: To reference the summary reports of the individual systems, and to record that the quality system elements are implemented and include a formal release statement
options.C: To replace the summary reports of all systems, so that individual system test reports no longer need to be kept and no source needs to be referenced
options.D: To list only the project's financial settlement and budget execution, unrelated to the quality system and release

questions.explanation: In this approach the summary report of each system documents test completion, and the overall report references them and records completion of the quality system elements and the formal release statement. The advantage is that tests can be closed early rather than waiting for procedures to be finalized. The disadvantage is that grouping may complicate later changes, and during an inspection data for the whole group of systems must be presented.

questions.question: When a new system is implemented in an existing facility under QA-managed Quality Change Control, how can the implementation of quality system elements and the formal release be documented?

options.A: It must be written in the Qualification Summary Report, and change control may not be used
options.B: No written record is needed; the using unit confirms verbally and notifies QA, and the system is released
options.C: It can be recorded in change control and referenced by the Qualification Summary Report
options.D: A statement from the supplier is enough, and the owner need not separately document implementation and release status

questions.explanation: Existing facilities often verify the implementation of quality system elements and document formal release in change control; in that case the Qualification Summary Report need only reference the change control record, which allows the testing phase to be closed in good time.

questions.question: What is the basic structure of the periodic review method proposed in this guide?

options.A: Two phases: first classify by impact on product quality and assign a frequency, then review level by level in Tiers A, B, and C
options.B: A detailed, comprehensive review of all systems every year, with no frequency distinction based on impact on product quality
options.C: A fixed-interval re-execution of the full IQ/OQ/PQ and reapproval of all validation documents and protocols, whether or not the system has changed
options.D: A single phase in which the supplier issues the review report directly and the owner only files it without evaluating it

questions.explanation: Phase 1 is system classification and scheduling, and Phase 2 is the execution of the three-tier review. The guide notes that the traditional approach of annual detailed review of change and maintenance records takes much effort for little return and buries important signals, so a triage-like approach is used instead to find abnormal signals.

questions.topic: Four quality systems in periodic review
questions.question: The three-tier evaluation in periodic review examines which four quality systems?

options.A: Supplier management, training, documentation, and internal audit
options.B: Procurement, warehousing, production scheduling, and complaints
options.C: Environmental monitoring, media fill, cleaning validation, and sterilization
options.D: GMP compliance, change control, maintenance/calibration, and deviation

questions.explanation: The four quality systems examined in the three-tier evaluation are GMP compliance expectations, the change control system, the maintenance/calibration system, and the deviation system, with the aim of finding any sign that the system is not continuing to maintain its qualified state.

questions.question: In the initial Tier A assessment of a system, no signs of inconsistent system operation are found in any of the four quality systems. What is the next step?

options.A: Still proceed to the detailed Tier B assessment
options.B: The review is regarded as complete
options.C: Proceed directly to Tier C and re-execute all tests
options.D: Schedule requalification, because the assessment period has been exceeded

questions.explanation: Tier A is a high-level initial assessment, and if no abnormal signals are found the review is complete. The review proceeds to Tier B only if the system may be operating inconsistently, and to Tier C only if concerns remain after Tier B. This is how the triage approach focuses effort on the systems that show signals.

questions.question: According to the examples in Table 9.1, what are the periodic revalidation frequencies for aseptic process simulation on an aseptic filling line and for all sterilization cycles of a steam sterilizer, respectively?

options.A: Both are once a year
options.B: Both are every six months
options.C: Aseptic process simulation on the filling line is every six months, and steam sterilizer sterilization cycles are once a year
options.D: Aseptic process simulation on the filling line is once a year, and steam sterilizer sterilization cycles are every six months

questions.explanation: Table 9.1 lists all sterilization cycles of a steam sterilizer, equipment SIP, and depyrogenation cycles of a depyrogenation tunnel as annual, and aseptic process simulation of an aseptic filling line as every six months. The table also reminds users to confirm local requirements.

questions.question: Critical utilities such as HVAC and purified water already undergo routine monitoring (review of results, reporting of performance trends and preventive maintenance/calibration indicators, and a check that drawings and labeling are current). What view does the guide take on additional periodic review?

options.A: No additional review is needed: monitoring confirms performance, and the drawing check confirms the documentation is current
options.B: A full three-tier Tier A, B, and C review of these systems is still required every year, with a report issued
options.C: A full PQ must still be re-executed every year, with all related protocols and reports reapproved
options.D: As long as routine monitoring exists, there is no need even to check separately or update whether drawings and labeling are current

questions.explanation: The guide states that when critical utilities already have routine monitoring, additional review is not considered necessary, because monitoring confirms system performance and the drawing check confirms the documentation is current. For other systems (such as manufacturing systems), review frequency is determined by relative risk to product quality.

questions.question: How does the vendor assessment in this guide, performed to use supplier documentation in support of C&Q, differ from an ordinary supplier audit?

options.A: They are completely the same, both intended to qualify the supplier and add it to the approved supplier list, so they can share one report
options.B: It applies only to suppliers of raw materials and packaging components, not to equipment and system suppliers
options.C: It can fully replace all the owner's testing, so the owner need not perform any verification
options.D: It evaluates whether the supplier's documentation and testing can support C&Q, and is not a supplier qualification or audit

questions.explanation: The guide explains that this kind of assessment is for the purpose of validation documentation, is not a vendor qualification/audit, and is also different from the product-focused assessment of raw material and packaging suppliers. The result is used to decide to what extent supplier documentation can be used, which reduces on-site testing and cost.

questions.question: For confirming the materials of product-contact parts, what view does the guide take if the supplier's quality is reliable?

options.A: 100% of heat certificates must always be checked, with QA signing off batch by batch
options.B: Supplier certificates of conformity may never be accepted; all product-contact materials must be sent by the owner for its own testing
options.C: A certificate of conformity from a good supplier can be accepted, without checking all the heat certificates
options.D: Certificates of conformity may be accepted only for non-product-contact materials; for product-contact materials, the manufacturer's certificates and heat treatment lot numbers must always be checked batch by batch

questions.explanation: The guide gives as an example that accepting a good supplier's certificate of conformity to confirm product-contact materials is an acceptable low-risk practice, so 100% of the related heat certificates need not be checked. This is an example of leveraging supplier expertise to reduce duplicate verification.

questions.question: A supplier does not normally operate in a GMP environment, and a QMS is unfamiliar to it. How should this be handled according to the guide?

options.A: Tell the supplier that its goods are for pharmaceutical use, identify shortfalls early, and add controls (such as training, additional review, and witnessing)
options.B: Do not work with such suppliers; choose a supplier that already has GMP experience and request new quotations
options.C: No special handling is needed; treat it like any other supplier under the normal purchasing process
options.D: The supplier trains its own staff, and the owner need not take part or separately verify the training results or request training records

questions.explanation: The guide asks that the supplier first be made aware that it is supplying a pharmaceutical company, that gaps be identified early, and that its cooperation be obtained before adding controls, such as supplier training, additional review or audits, witnessing of critical stages, or additional owner testing to compensate for parts where supplier test documentation cannot be relied on.

questions.question: In the typical document hierarchy of a quality system described in Chapter 11, which is the order from top to bottom?

options.A: Executable documents (plans, test scripts, reports), then procedures, then standards, with policy/directive at the very top
options.B: Policy/directive, then standards, then procedures, with executable documents (plans, test scripts, reports) at the bottom
options.C: Standards, then policy/directive, then procedures, with executable documents (plans, test scripts, reports) at the bottom
options.D: All documents are at the same level with no hierarchy, distinguished only by document number and approval date

questions.explanation: At the top is the policy/directive, which records the organization's expectations; next are standards, which set the minimum deliverables and prevent departments from interpreting the policy's intent differently; then procedures; and at the bottom are executable documents such as plans, test scripts, and reports.

questions.question: Under what circumstances can a project waive a formal vendor assessment?

options.A: Never; all suppliers must complete a formal assessment regardless of risk
options.B: Whenever the supplier gives the lowest quote and shortest lead time, decided directly by purchasing with no Quality Unit involvement
options.C: The project manager may decide alone, with no written rationale and no Quality Unit approval
options.D: Based on the supplier's current qualification, history of use, prior audits, or a written rationale approved by the Quality Unit

questions.explanation: The guide lists the grounds for waiver: the supplier's current qualification status, history of use, prior audits, the information supplied not being critical, or other documented rationale approved by the Quality Unit. Whether to reassess a supplier already assessed is also decided on risk, using the same factors as the initial assessment.

questions.topic: Start of QA-managed Quality Change Control
questions.question: In a C&Q project, between SME-led ECM and QA-managed Quality Change Control (QCC), at what earliest point does QA-managed QCC apply?

options.A: From the very start of the conceptual design phase, continuing throughout the project lifecycle until system retirement, with all changes requiring QA approval
options.B: Only from the Acceptance and release stage
options.C: From the day detailed design is complete, with all design changes requiring QA approval
options.D: From the start of commissioning, with all commissioning changes pre-approved by QA

questions.explanation: The guide advocates SME-led ECM before acceptance and release, with QA-managed QCC starting at the earliest at the acceptance and release stage, so that change management does not become a barrier to innovation. However, changes to the design, function, or acceptance criteria of CAs/CDEs still need Quality Unit approval before verification testing.

questions.question: After a system is released into commercial production, a part of the same specification and model is to be replaced on site (like-for-like), a category already approved in the validation documents. How should this be viewed according to the guide?

options.A: It is one of the situations (like-for-like) that can be handled by ECM without Quality Unit involvement
options.B: It must always be pre-approved through QA-managed QCC and may not be handled directly by the SME
options.C: Full revalidation must always be repeated, with all validation documents and protocols reapproved and the system rereleased by the Quality Unit
options.D: PQ must be redone and the URS updated, with Quality Unit release obtained again

questions.explanation: After release, changes that affect product quality in principle require pre-approval through QA-managed QCC, but the guide also explains that some situations can use ECM without Quality Unit involvement, such as like-for-like replacements that have been documented and approved in the validation documents. The guide also notes that replacing a part with one identical to the original is not necessarily regarded as a change.

questions.question: According to Good Documentation Practice, when an error is found in a C&Q test record, which correction method is consistent with the guide?

options.A: Cover the original entry with correction fluid and rewrite it, then add initials and date beside it
options.B: Overwrite the original directly with the new figure, then add initials and date beside it
options.C: Strike through the entire number or word, not just one character of it, and add an explanation if the reason is not obvious
options.D: Erase the original entry with an eraser and fill it in again, then add the correction date and the initials of the person making the correction at the foot of the page

questions.explanation: The guide states that original records must not be erased, overwritten, or obscured, and correction fluid must not be used. A correction is made by striking through the entire number or word, and if the reason is not obvious, a unique identifier and an explanation are added.

questions.question: After a test document has been approved, how should "N/A" be marked in an unused field according to the guide?

options.A: No additional record is needed; simply writing N/A is treated as complete
options.B: Change it to "N/AV" and leave it to the user whether to add an explanation
options.C: The Quality Unit must reapprove the whole document and issue a new version
options.D: After approval, N/A usually needs an explanation, initials, and date

questions.explanation: "N/A" should be used only before approval for execution; using N/A after the document is approved generally requires an explanation, initials, and date. The guide also reminds users to distinguish N/A (not applicable) from N/AV (not available).

questions.question: When the result of a test step is quantitative data, how should it be recorded in the results column?

options.A: Write "OK" to indicate it meets expectations, then add initials and date beside it
options.B: Record the actual observed value, and do not write only Pass, OK, Yes, or a tick
options.C: Write only Pass or Fail, with no need to record the actual value, to avoid overly long records
options.D: Copy the wording of the expected result in the acceptance criterion word for word, without recording the measured value

questions.explanation: For quantitative results the actual number must be recorded; Pass, Fail, As Expected, Same, OK, Yes, or a tick are all unacceptable ways of recording. The guide also explains that the expected result need not be copied word for word; it is enough to record the observed system response in clear wording.

questions.question: When an organization moves to this guide's science- and risk-based C&Q approach, what happens to the existing completed validation documents?

options.A: All become invalid, and complete revalidation of every existing system must be performed under the new approach and reapproved
options.B: All must have a System Risk Assessment added and be reapproved before they can continue to be used
options.C: They do not become invalid; validation documents are a snapshot of the system at a point in time and can continue to serve as evidence of fitness for intended use
options.D: Only documents completed within two years and reapproved by the Quality Unit are valid

questions.explanation: The guide states clearly that adopting the new approach does not invalidate existing work or documents. Validation documents represent the state at a point in time, and later changes are managed by quality systems such as change management, maintenance, calibration, and periodic review, so existing documents can still serve as evidence that the system is fit for intended use.

questions.question: For existing systems, what does the guide consider the most cost-effective way to implement the approach?

options.A: Revalidate all systems at once and revise all documents within a year
options.B: Suspend use of the systems until all documents have been completed under the new approach and reapproved
options.C: Downgrade all existing systems to not direct impact to avoid producing documents
options.D: Supplement existing practice gradually when gaps are found or systems are changed, to make maximum use of existing documentation

questions.explanation: The guide considers the most cost-effective approach to be to progressively strengthen traditional practice as gaps are found or systems change, so as to make maximum use of existing documents. If a system has no potential to impact product quality, it can be reclassified and receive commissioning only.

questions.question: Before implementing the approach in this guide, what preparation does the guide recommend?

options.A: First perform a documented organizational maturity assessment; a small proof-of-concept project can identify what needs strengthening, and senior management support is obtained
options.B: Switch the whole company over at once with no pilot, and without assessing whether the organization's existing maturity and resources are sufficient
options.C: Update only the Quality department's SOPs, with no separate action for other departments and suppliers
options.D: First stop all ongoing projects and wait until regulations are updated and the authority reissues the guidance

questions.explanation: The guide recommends a documented assessment of organizational maturity (covering the quality system and GEP, and looking at R&D, Quality, Engineering, system owners, and so on), a clear implementation strategy, and senior management support; a small proof-of-concept project helps identify what needs strengthening.

questions.question: An existing system has the potential to impact product quality, but its existing validation documents do not meet current expectations. How should this be handled according to the guide?

options.A: Leave things as they are and do nothing until the next regulatory inspection
options.B: Qualify the system under the new approach and fill the gaps
options.C: Simply reclassify it as not direct impact to avoid having to produce documents
options.D: Perform only periodic review, with no action on the documentation gaps

questions.explanation: The guide's best practice is to first determine whether the system has the potential to impact product quality: if not, reclassify it and perform commissioning only; if so, review the existing documents, and where they do not meet current expectations, qualify the system under the new approach and fill the gaps.

questions.question: Appendix 1 cites the statement "QRM should be applied throughout the lifecycle of a product, and the scope and extent of validation should be based on a justified and documented risk assessment." Which document does this come from?

options.A: EU GMP Annex 3 and PIC/S Annex 3 (radiopharmaceuticals) and related annexes
options.B: The FDA 2011 Process Validation guidance
options.C: EU GMP Annex 15 and PIC/S Annex 15
options.D: ASTM E2500-13

questions.explanation: This text is quoted from EU GMP Annex 15 and PIC/S Annex 15; PIC/S adopted the EU Annex 15, and from Version 12 the two have identical content. The FDA 2011 guidance is the source of a different quotation, and the guide notes that ASTM E2500-13 can serve as a useful reference.
